title: Peer Review Feedback Examples: 100 Phrases for Positive and Constructive Feedback

In 30 seconds


### TL;DR


- Peer review feedback is input colleagues at the same level give each other on work quality, skills, and behavior.
- This guide has 100 examples: 30 positive, 40 constructive, 10 strengths and weaknesses pairs, 8 quick competency pairs, and 12 examples by role.
- Strong peer feedback names a specific behavior, its effect, and one next step.
- Use start-stop-continue or the free template below to structure your review.
- Keep comments about the work, not the person, and follow up after you share them.


Peer review feedback is input that colleagues at the same level give each other about work quality, skills, and behavior. It recognizes what is working and flags what to improve, usually as part of a performance review or 360 feedback cycle.


Below are 100 peer review feedback examples you can copy and adapt: positive and constructive phrases sorted by competency and by role, plus a step-by-step method for writing your own and a free template.


## 30 Positive Peer Review Examples by Competency


A positive peer review example names the colleague, the specific behavior, and the result it produced. Specific praise tells the person what to repeat, while generic praise like “great job” gives them nothing to act on. The 30 examples below cover eight competencies, so you can jump to the skill you want to recognize.


Competency Positive peer review example


Work quality “Kudos to Sarah for consistently delivering high-quality reports that impress both clients and colleagues. Her attention to detail and creative problem-solving set the bar for the team.”


Work quality “John’s attention to detail and commitment to excellence make his work the standard for the team. His consistent, high-quality contributions keep our projects on track.”


Work quality “Alexandra holds every project to its quality standards and sets the benchmark for the department. She regularly goes the extra mile to check the final output.”


Work quality “Patrick ships clean, error-free code. His precise coding and knack for spotting bugs early save the team hours of rework.”


Job skills “Michael’s knowledge and problem-solving skills helped us clear some of our hardest technical hurdles. He breaks complex issues down and finds creative solutions. Great job, Michael!”


Job skills “Emily grasps complex concepts quickly and applies them to her work. Her knack for simplifying the intricate helps the whole team.”

## 40 Constructive Peer Review Feedback Examples


Constructive peer review feedback names one behavior to change, explains its effect on the work or the team, and suggests a next step. Opening with a real strength and ending with a suggestion keeps the comment fair without sounding harsh. These 40 peer review comments cover the same eight competencies as the positive examples.


Competency Constructive peer review example


Work quality “I appreciate John’s attention to detail on our projects. I noticed a few typos in his recent report, so I’d suggest an extra proofreading pass before he shares final drafts.”


Work quality “Sarah’s research is thorough and her insights are useful. For clarity and brevity, I recommend she distill her conclusions to the most essential points.”


Work quality “Michael’s coding skills are strong. To help team collaboration, I’d suggest he add more detailed comments in his code so it is easier to read and maintain.”


Work quality “Emma’s creative design concepts are inspiring. Using consistent color schemes across projects would strengthen brand recognition.”


Work quality “David’s analysis is thorough. Presenting the data in a more reader-friendly format would help everyone understand it faster.”


Job skills “Megan’s technical skills are solid. To keep growing, I recommend she take on more challenging projects that stretch her expertise.”


Job skills “Robert’s industry knowledge is extensive. To become more well-rounded, I’d suggest he focus on his client relationship and communication skills.”


Job skills “Alice handles complex projects well. I’d recommend she sharpen her risk assessment skills so she can catch potential issues earlier.”


Job skills “Daniel’s presentations are excellent and his reports are informative. There is room to improve in interpreting data and turning it into actionable insights.”


Job skills “Laura’s sales techniques work, and she consistently meets her targets. I encourage her to build her negotiation skills to close bigger deals and partnerships.”


Leadership “James makes sound decisions. To build a more inclusive team, I’d suggest he ask for input from team members before decisions are final.”


Leadership “Sophia delegates efficiently and her team trusts her. To inspire the team further, I’d suggest she share credit more generously and acknowledge the collective effort.”


Leadership “Nathan’s vision and strategic thinking are clear. Building his conflict resolution skills would help keep the team focused when disagreements come up.”


Leadership “Olivia’s accountability is appreciated. I’d encourage her to strengthen her mentoring approach to develop the team’s potential further.”


Leadership “Ethan’s adaptability brings agility to the team. A more motivational leadership style would lift team morale during demanding projects.”


Teamwork “Ava’s collaboration is key to the team’s success. She should consider speaking up more in group discussions so we hear her insights.”


Teamwork “Liam is a strong team player, and he could motivate peers further by sharing credit more openly and recognizing their contributions.”


Teamwork “Chloe’s flexibility is a big help to the team. Practicing active listening in meetings would make her an even more effective teammate.”


Teamwork “William’s contributions to group projects are consistently valuable. To widen his impact, I suggest he join cross-functional projects with other departments.”


Teamwork “Zoe handles conflict calmly. Building her mediation skills to find solutions that work for both sides would strengthen team cohesion.”


Professionalism “Noah’s punctuality is an asset to the team. Meeting every project deadline with the same consistency would make him a model for his peers.”


Professionalism “Grace’s integrity and ethical standards are admirable. I’d recommend more discretion when discussing sensitive matters in open channels.”


Professionalism “Logan’s work ethic is strong and his commitment is clear. Sharing project updates with colleagues more often would keep everyone informed.”


Professionalism “Sophie is reliable. Paying closer attention to confidentiality when handling sensitive information would strengthen her professionalism.”


Professionalism “Jackson’s organizational skills are top-notch. Keeping his shared workspace and files as tidy as his plans would help the team find what they need.”


Mentoring “Aiden provides valuable mentoring to junior team members. He could set aside regular time for guidance to help them navigate their careers.”

Mentoring “Ella’s mentorship plays a key role in her colleagues’ growth. She could expand it to long-term career guidance, helping them set and reach professional goals.”


Mentoring “Benjamin’s helpfulness creates a supportive atmosphere. He could encourage team members to ask for help early instead of waiting until they are stuck.”


Communication “Mia communicates clearly. To reach different audiences, she could use a wider mix of channels, such as short videos or written summaries.”


Communication “Lucas articulates ideas well and his verbal communication is strong. He could work on his body language so it matches his spoken message.”

## Peer Review Strengths and Weaknesses Examples


Peer review strengths and weaknesses examples pair one thing a colleague does well with one area to develop, so the review stays balanced. Frame the weakness as a skill to build, not a flaw, and link it to the strength where you can. Use these 10 pairs when a review form asks for both.


Strength phrasing Paired development phrasing


“Breaks complex problems into clear steps the rest of the team can follow.” “Could share their reasoning earlier, before the solution is final, so others can add input.”


“Delivers accurate work that rarely needs a second review.” “Could hand off drafts sooner; waiting for a perfect version slows down the people who depend on the work.”


“Stays calm and focused when priorities change mid-sprint.” “Could flag the trade-offs of a priority change to stakeholders instead of quietly absorbing the extra load.”


“Builds strong relationships with clients and partners.” “Could document client agreements in writing so the team has a shared record.”


“Gives teammates thoughtful, specific feedback in code and design reviews.” “Could balance critique with recognition so newer teammates know what to keep doing.”


“Takes ownership of problems and follows them through to the end.” “Could delegate more of the follow-up work so they are not the single point of failure.”


“Brings creative ideas to brainstorming sessions.” “Could narrow ideas to one or two with a clear plan before presenting them for a decision.”


“Writes clear, well-organized documentation.” “Could speak up more in live meetings, where many decisions get made.”


“Responds quickly to requests from other teams.” “Could protect focus time for deep work instead of switching to every new message.”


“Mentors new hires patiently through their first weeks.” “Could set clearer expectations and check-in points so mentees know how they are progressing.”

Competency Positive phrase Constructive phrase


Work quality “Consistently delivers accurate, thorough work and catches issues before they reach the customer.” “Could build in a final check to catch small errors before handoff.”

## Peer Review Examples by Role: Manager, Coworker, and Direct Report


Peer review examples by role adjust the tone to the working relationship. Feedback for a manager is upward, so it focuses on the support and clarity you need. Feedback for a coworker is lateral and centers on collaboration. Feedback for a direct report is downward and ties to goals and growth. These 12 examples cover all three.


Who you are reviewing Direction Example


Manager Upward “Your weekly one-on-ones give me clear priorities. Sharing the reasoning behind roadmap changes earlier would help me plan my work.”


Manager Upward “You protect the team from last-minute scope changes, which keeps our sprints predictable.”


Manager Upward “Feedback on my work closer to delivery, rather than at the quarterly review, would help me correct course sooner.”


Manager Upward “You recognize individual contributions in team meetings, which keeps morale high.”


Coworker or peer Lateral “Working with you on the launch was easy because you shared progress daily and flagged risks early.”


Coworker or peer Lateral “Your code reviews are thorough and kind. Adding a short summary at the top would help me prioritize the changes.”


Coworker or peer Lateral “You always make time to help when I’m stuck. Looping me into decisions that affect my part of the project would help us avoid rework.”


Coworker or peer Lateral “In client calls, you set up my sections well, which makes our joint presentations run smoothly.”


Direct report Downward “You hit every milestone on the onboarding project. Next quarter, I’d like to see you own the stakeholder updates too.”


Direct report Downward “Your analysis shaped our pricing decision. Leading with the key finding on the first slide would help it land faster with leadership.”


Direct report Downward “You’ve grown a lot in handling customer escalations. Documenting how you resolved them would help the rest of the team.”


Direct report Downward “You take on extra work willingly. Let’s agree on priorities each week so your core goals don’t slip.”


When feedback comes from all three directions at once, it becomes a 360 review. See these[360 degree feedback examples](https://www.peoplebox.ai/blog/360-degree-feedback-examples/) for multi-rater phrasing.


## How to Write and Give Peer Review Feedback


To write good peer review feedback, gather specific examples, describe the behavior and its effect, tie it to a competency, balance strengths with one or two areas to improve, and end with a clear suggestion. Keep the tone kind and the focus on the work. Then follow up so the feedback turns into action.


1. **Collect specific examples first.** Before you write, list two or three moments from recent projects. Notes from the whole review period protect you from recency bias.
2. **Describe the behavior and its effect.** Say what the person did and what happened as a result. “Your daily status notes kept the launch on schedule” beats “great communicator.”
3. **Tie each point to a competency.** Link your comment to a skill such as communication, teamwork, or time management, so it lines up with how performance is assessed.
4. **Balance positive and constructive.** Start with a real strength, then name one or two areas to develop. More than that overwhelms the reader.
5. **Use start-stop-continue for structure.** Suggest one thing to start, one to stop, and one to continue. For example: “Start sharing drafts earlier, stop rewriting slides the night before, continue running the weekly sync.”
6. **Make it kind, actionable, and followed up.** Phrase suggestions as next steps, avoid personal remarks, and check in a few weeks later to see what changed.

## Do’s and Don’ts of Peer Review Feedback


The best peer review feedback is specific, evidence-based, timely, and focused on the work. The most common mistakes are vague praise, personal criticism, recency bias, and a long list of changes with no follow-up. Use the two lists below as a final check before you submit a review.


**Do’s of peer review feedback**


- **Empathize and relate.** Put yourself in the recipient’s shoes. Recognize the effort behind the work and frame comments with care.
- **Ground feedback in evidence.** Base every point on concrete examples from the work, so the recipient knows exactly where to improve.
- **Write clearly and concisely.** Use plain language and skip jargon that could be misread.
- **Offer a path forward.** Pair each criticism with a possible solution or alternative.
- **Highlight strengths.** Name what is done well so the person knows what to build on.
- **Keep it timely.** Share feedback while the work is still fresh, not months later.


**Don’ts of peer review feedback**


- **Don’t be vague.** Comments like “It’s not good” give no direction. Name the specific behavior.
- **Don’t make it personal.** Critique the work and its outcome, never the individual.
- **Don’t rely on subjective opinions.** Stick to observable behavior and agreed criteria.
- **Don’t overload with suggestions.** One or two clear priorities help more than a long list.
- **Don’t let recency bias decide.** Review the whole period, not only the last few weeks.
- **Don’t skip the follow-up.** Check that the feedback was understood and is being applied.


**A note on anonymity:** many teams run peer reviews anonymously so reviewers can be candid without straining working relationships. Anonymous feedback still needs to be specific and respectful, because the recipient cannot ask the reviewer for context.


## Tools to Collect and Compile Peer Feedback


Writing one peer review is manageable. Running peer reviews across a whole team is harder: you need to pick the right reviewers, keep responses anonymous, chase late submissions, and compile many reviewers into one clear view per employee. That is the job 360 feedback software does. Look for these capabilities:


- **Reviewer selection:** employees or managers can nominate the peers best placed to give feedback.
- **Configurable anonymity:** HR decides what reviewers and recipients can see.
- **Customizable forms:** competency-based questions and templates like the one above.
- **Collection where people work:** reviews and reminders inside the chat tools your team already uses.
- **Compiled reports:** feedback from many reviewers rolled into one summary a manager can discuss.

## Frequently Asked Questions


### What is peer review feedback?


Peer review feedback is input that colleagues at the same level give each other about work quality, skills, and behavior. It recognizes what is working and flags what to improve, usually as part of a performance review or 360 feedback cycle. Because peers see day-to-day work that managers often miss, their feedback adds detail a manager review alone cannot. The goal is development: helping a colleague understand their impact and grow in their role.


### What are three positive peer review examples?


Three positive peer review examples: “Patrick ships clean, error-free code, and his knack for spotting bugs early saves the team hours of rework.” “Grace’s clear communication keeps our team’s objectives aligned; she explains complex ideas in a plain, direct way.” “Ben’s patience with new team members makes it easy for our junior colleagues to learn.” Each one names the person, a specific behavior, and the effect it had. That structure is what makes praise useful, because it tells the colleague exactly what to keep doing. Generic lines like “great job” feel nice but give the recipient nothing to repeat.


### How do you give good peer review feedback?


To give good peer review feedback, start with specific examples from the review period, not memory of the last few weeks. Describe what the person did and the effect it had, then tie it to a competency such as communication or teamwork. Balance one or two strengths with one or two areas to improve, and end with a clear, actionable suggestion. Keep the focus on the work rather than the person, and use plain language. A start-stop-continue structure helps if you are unsure where to begin. Finally, follow up a few weeks later to see whether the feedback was useful.


### Can you give an example of peer-to-peer feedback?


Here is a peer-to-peer feedback example that balances praise and a suggestion: “Working with you on the launch was easy because you shared progress daily and flagged risks early. One thing that would help: looping me into decisions that affect my part of the project, so we avoid rework.” It works because it names a specific behavior, explains why it mattered, and offers one clear next step. Peer-to-peer feedback is lateral, so the tone is collaborative rather than evaluative. It focuses on how two colleagues work together, not on ratings or pay decisions.


### What should you write in a peer review?


A peer review should cover three things: strengths, areas to improve, and one concrete suggestion. Under strengths, name two or three specific behaviors and the results they produced. Under areas to improve, pick one or two skills that would raise the person’s impact, framed as growth rather than failure. Then add a suggestion they can act on, such as a habit to start or a tool to try. Tie each point to a competency so it lines up with how performance is assessed. Keep it focused on observable work, not personality.


### How do you write constructive peer feedback without being harsh?


To write constructive peer feedback without being harsh, open with a real strength, describe the specific behavior you want to change, and explain its effect on the work or the team. Then offer a suggestion instead of a verdict. For example: “Michael’s coding skills are strong. Adding more detailed comments in his code would make it easier for the team to maintain.” Use “could” and “would help” rather than “always” or “never.” Critique the work, not the person, and limit yourself to one or two points so the feedback feels manageable.


### What is the difference between peer feedback and a manager review?


Peer feedback comes from colleagues at the same level, while a manager review comes from the person someone reports to. Peers see day-to-day collaboration, communication, and teamwork that a manager may not observe directly. A manager review usually carries more weight in formal decisions such as ratings, promotions, and pay, and it measures progress against goals. Peer feedback is typically developmental and adds context to the manager’s view. Many companies combine both, along with self and upward feedback, in a 360 review.


### Can peer reviews be anonymous?


Yes, peer reviews can be anonymous, and many organizations run them that way so reviewers can be candid without worrying about their working relationships. Anonymity works best when a team has enough reviewers that individual responses cannot be identified. The trade-off is that the recipient cannot ask for context, so anonymous feedback needs to be specific, behavior-based, and respectful. Some teams use a middle ground: names are hidden from the recipient but visible to HR or the manager, which helps prevent misuse.


### How long should peer review feedback be?


Peer review feedback is usually most useful at three to six sentences per competency, or a short paragraph overall. That is long enough to name a specific behavior, its effect, and one suggestion, and short enough that the recipient reads all of it. Concise peer review feedback beats a long list, because one or two clear priorities are easier to act on than ten loose comments. If the form has separate boxes for strengths and improvements, two or three sentences in each is a good target.


### Are there peer review examples for nurses?


Yes. Nursing peer review follows a different structure from general workplace peer review, because it focuses on clinical practice, patient safety, and professional standards. The examples on this page are written for office and corporate teams, so they will not cover clinical competencies.
